records.place: The Regaleali estate in the inland hills, Contea di Sclafani DOC, Sicily

wine.name: Rosso del Conte
wine.classification: Denominazione di Origine Controllata, the rank below DOCG
wine.grapes: Nero d'Avola, more than half in the vintages of the late 2010s, with Perricone for the rest; some older vintages took in other red grapes of the estate.
wine.sites: The San Lucio vineyard at Regaleali, about 480 metres up and facing south on sandy loam with some limestone: Perricone and Nero d'Avola planted mixed in 1959, with a block of Nero d'Avola alone added in 1965.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel, starting cool and finishing warmer, with about twenty days on the skins and a full malolactic. The wine then spends about eighteen months in new 225 litre barriques of French oak from Allier and Tronçais before bottling, by the house's sheet for the 2019 vintage.
wine.glass: Black cherry, red plum and carob over liquorice, tobacco leaf, dried Mediterranean herbs and the vanilla and clove of new oak; full and warm, with ripe, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, dusty finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and oaky when young, it opens after five years or so and can keep for two decades and more in a strong vintage, turning towards leather and dried fig.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The DOC of the high inland hills in which the Regaleali estate lies.
The family's estate in the interior, bought in 1830, where the wine is grown.
The count's red: the name the wine took after it was first sold as Riserva del Conte.

records.table: Tasca d'Almerita's Rosso del Conte is Nero d'Avola with Perricone from the San Lucio vineyard, planted in 1959 on the Regaleali estate high in the island's interior. Black cherry, carob and firm tannin after eighteen months in new oak: decant it, and pour it with lamb.
records.story: In 1830 two brothers of the Tasca family bought Regaleali, a great estate in the hills of the island's interior, between Palermo and Caltanissetta. As the house tells it, the land reform of the 1950s took more than half of the estate. In 1959 the count who then led the family planted Perricone and Nero d'Avola together on the hill of San Lucio. The vineyard gave a red of its own with the 1970 vintage, sold as Riserva del Conte and later named Rosso del Conte, the count's red, and the house calls it the first single vineyard wine of Sicily. At a time when much of the island's red left it in bulk, Regaleali bottled a Sicilian red from one vineyard, made to keep. The count's son later planted international varieties at Regaleali, and the family went on to vineyards on Etna, on Salina and on the island of Mozia. Rosso del Conte is the bottle that shows a guest the inland Sicily: high, far from the sea, and a red that rewards years in the cellar.

others.name: Riserva del Conte
others.note: The old name, made again from the same vineyard from the 2010 vintage after forty years, and aged in 500 litre chestnut barrels.

others.name: Nozze d'Oro
others.note: The estate's white, Inzolia with a local selection of Sauvignon.

others.name: Tascante
others.note: The family's Nerello Mascalese from Etna.

traps: Regaleali is the estate and Tasca d'Almerita the family: a bottle may carry both names, and the flagship is Rosso del Conte.
Rosso del Conte was at first sold as Riserva del Conte; the house brought that name back with the 2010 vintage for a separate, chestnut aged wine of the same vineyard.
Rosso del Conte is Nero d'Avola with Perricone from the inland hills, not with Frappato, which is the partner of Cerasuolo di Vittoria.

cards.front: Tasca d'Almerita's Rosso del Conte: which vineyard gives it, and when was it planted?
cards.back: San Lucio at Regaleali, planted with Perricone and Nero d'Avola together in 1959.

cards.front: Under what name was the first vintage of Rosso del Conte, the 1970, sold?
cards.back: Riserva del Conte; the wine was later named Rosso del Conte, the count's red.

questions.q: A guest asks which grapes make Tasca d'Almerita's Rosso del Conte. What do you tell them?
opts: Nero d'Avola with Perricone
Nero d'Avola with Frappato
Nerello Mascalese with Nerello Cappuccio
Nero d'Avola with Cabernet Sauvignon
questions.exp: The San Lucio vineyard was planted with Perricone and Nero d'Avola together in 1959; Nero d'Avola with Frappato is the blend of Cerasuolo di Vittoria, from the south east.

questions.q: Which estate in the hills of the interior did two brothers of the Tasca family buy in 1830?
opts: Regaleali
Mozia
Contessa Entellina
Samperi
questions.exp: The brothers bought Regaleali in 1830, and Rosso del Conte grows on its San Lucio hill; Contessa Entellina is Donnafugata's estate, and Mozia an island where the family came later.

report: Searches for this record: five of the group's 35 (two on the house's domain, one on five trade domains, two open); the house's history page, Rosso del Conte page and 2019 and 2018 sheets, and its Riserva del Conte sheet for the 2016, were read through search summaries.

The purchase of 1830 by the brothers Lucio and Carmelo Mastrogiovanni Tasca rests on the house's history page and Terra Madre; neither gives the brothers' dates, so they are described. The count who planted San Lucio in 1959 is Giuseppe Tasca d'Almerita in every source, but no source read gave his dates, so he is described, not named; his son Lucio's death was reported by The Drinks Business in July 2022, and he too is described.

The 1970 first vintage rests on the house and two secondary accounts; the house's history page has it sold as the 1970 while its Italian sustainability report says it reached the market six years later, and one tour page gives 1976, so the record says only that the 1970 was the first vintage. The name Riserva del Conte for the first wines rests on the house's page and Terra Madre.

The count's resolve, late in the 1960s, to make a reserve red that could age like the long lived reds abroad rests on Terra Madre alone and is left out; the first single vineyard wine of Sicily is the house's own claim and is told as such, and the story no longer says the first vintages were aged in oak, since no source read gave their vessels.

San Lucio's height, aspect, soil, the plantings of 1959 and 1965, the twenty days on the skins and the eighteen months in new Allier and Tronçais barriques are the house's 2019 sheet; the blend was 53 per cent Nero d'Avola that year, while the library calls the wine Nero d'Avola led, so the record says close to equal shares in recent sheets.

The library's note says first made in the 1970s, which agrees; the region record's producers line calls Rosso del Conte an early benchmark for Nero d'Avola, a judgement word not repeated here, and gives Perricone no place, though every source read names it as a partner.
Left out for want of a source: the year of the Contea di Sclafani DOC, the Lucio Tasca company founded in 1961 (one tribute only), and a comparison with Sassicaia's first release made by one critic.

changed: wine.grapes: "the house's recent sheets give them close to equal shares"; now "Nero d'Avola, more than half in the vintages of the late 2010s, with Perricone for the rest; some older vintages took in other red grapes of the estate", since the sheets and merchants read give 53 to 62 per cent Nero d'Avola for 2017 to 2019 (superiore.de, xtraWine, Wine Review Online) and other estate reds in the 2012 and 2016 (Carta dei Vini, Sapori del Belice).

wine.sites: "facing south and south west" and "bush vines planted mixed in 1959, with more Nero d'Avola added in 1965"; now "facing south" and "Perricone and Nero d'Avola planted mixed in 1959, with a block of Nero d'Avola alone added in 1965": the house's documents give south south east on most and south west on one, and its own narrative has the 1965 block of Nero d'Avola alone; no source read gave the training, so bush vines is cut.

story and cards[0].back: "together as bush vines" and "mixed Perricone and Nero d'Avola bush vines"; now "together", for the same reason: the house's pages read give the planting of 1959 but not how the vines were trained.

others[0].note: "mostly Perricone and aged in new chestnut barrels, by the house's sheet for the 2016"; now "made again from the same vineyard from the 2010 vintage after forty years, and aged in 500 litre chestnut barrels": the house's pages disagree on the blend (Perricone 60 per cent on one, Nero d'Avola 60 per cent on its shop page) and give the return of 2010 and the 500 litre chestnut.
traps[1]: "a separate, Perricone led wine"; now "brought that name back with the 2010 vintage for a separate, chestnut aged wine", for the same reason.
open: Falstaff and two merchants list some vintages of Rosso del Conte as Sicilia DOC rather than Contea di Sclafani DOC; the house's own pages and most merchants give Contea di Sclafani, which the record keeps, but the label of a given vintage may differ.
The count who planted San Lucio in 1959 and the brothers of 1830 stay described, not named, for want of their dates in two sources.

records.place: Pantelleria, the volcanic island off Tunisia, Passito di Pantelleria DOC, Sicily

wine.name: Ben Ryé Passito di Pantelleria
wine.classification: Denominazione di Origine Controllata, for the island's sweet wine of dried Zibibbo
wine.grapes: Zibibbo alone, the Muscat of Alexandria of Pantelleria.
wine.sites: Low bush vines of Zibibbo, each set in a hollow dug against the wind, on terraces walled with dry stone across several contrade of the house's vineyards on Pantelleria, a volcanic island closer to Tunisia than to Sicily.
wine.making: Picked in two passes. From August, grapes of an early picking are laid out to dry in the sun and wind; later grapes are pressed for a fresh must, and the dried ones, stripped from their stalks by hand, are added to it in batches as it ferments in stainless steel, a month and more in all. The wine then rests some months in tank and ten months or more in bottle, by the house's sheets.
wine.glass: Dried apricot, fig and date over candied orange peel, honey and saffron, with a lift of thyme and a salty edge; sweet and dense, kept fresh by bright acidity, with a long finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fragrant from release, it deepens towards date, toffee and walnut over a decade and more in bottle.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, or a little warmer to open its perfume; no need to decant; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The sweet wine of Zibibbo grown on Pantelleria, made in part from grapes dried in the sun.
From the Arabic for son of the wind, for the wind that sweeps the island's vines.
The DOC rank: grown and made under the rules of the island's denomination.

records.table: Donnafugata's Ben Ryé is Passito di Pantelleria: Zibibbo from low bush vines on a windswept volcanic island, part of it dried in the sun and added to the fermenting must. Apricot, fig and honey with a salty freshness: pour it cold beside blue cheese or almond pastry.
records.story: The Rallo family of Marsala had long made wine there, and its old cellars in the town date, by the house's account, from 1851. In 1983 Giacomo Rallo (1937 to 2016) and his wife founded Donnafugata, with the family's vineyards at Contessa Entellina, which she had taken in hand a few years before. She chose the name from the novel The Leopard: Donnafugata, the woman in flight, recalls, as the house tells it, a Bourbon queen who fled Naples and found refuge on the lands where its vineyards lie. In 1989 the house came to Pantelleria, the volcanic island off Tunisia where Zibibbo grows as low bush vines in hollows dug against the wind, and that year it made the first Ben Ryé, son of the wind in Arabic. In 2008 it restored a walled Pantellerian garden at Khamma and gave it to FAI, the Italian national trust, and in 2014 UNESCO inscribed the island's way of growing its bush vines as intangible cultural heritage of humanity. Giacomo Rallo died in 2016, and his children took the house on. Ben Ryé is the bottle to pour when a guest asks for the sweet wine of the Sicilian islands: grapes dried by sun and wind on a small island, kept fresh by bright acidity.

others.name: Mille e una Notte
others.note: The house's red from Contessa Entellina, led by Nero d'Avola.

others.name: Tancredi
others.note: Nero d'Avola with Cabernet Sauvignon, a long running blend of the house.

traps: Zibibbo on Pantelleria is Muscat of Alexandria, not Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.
Passito di Pantelleria and Moscato di Pantelleria are separate styles of the same grape under the island's rules, so name the passito in full.
Donnafugata is a name taken from a novel, not a place on Pantelleria: the house began at Marsala and Contessa Entellina in western Sicily.

cards.front: Donnafugata's Ben Ryé: how are the sun dried grapes used?
cards.back: Zibibbo dried in the sun and wind is added in batches to fresh must as it ferments in steel.

cards.front: What does the name Ben Ryé mean, and what was its first vintage?
cards.back: Son of the wind, from the Arabic; the first vintage was 1989, the year Donnafugata came to Pantelleria.

questions.q: A guest asks how Donnafugata gives Ben Ryé its richness. Which method fits?
opts: Sun dried Zibibbo added to fermenting fresh must
Grapes left on the vine until noble rot sets in
Grapes frozen on the vine before pressing
Grape spirit added to stop the fermentation
questions.exp: Grapes dried in the sun and wind are added in batches to fresh must as it ferments; the house's sheets give no noble rot and no added spirit.

questions.q: One of Donnafugata's founders chose the house's name in 1983. Where does it come from?
opts: The novel The Leopard
A contrada on Pantelleria
The Arabic for son of the wind
A Marsala merchant of 1851
questions.exp: The founder's wife took it from The Leopard, and the house ties its meaning, the woman in flight, to a fleeing queen; son of the wind is the meaning of Ben Ryé.

report: Searches for this record: six of the group's 35 (three on the house's domain, one on UNESCO's, two open); the house's roots and company pages and its Ben Ryé sheets for 2008, 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2023 were read through search summaries.

Giacomo Rallo's death on 10 May 2016 aged 79 rests on Decanter and The Drinks Business; his birth in Marsala in 1937 on one account (Palate Press), which the age agrees with, so the dates are given as 1937 to 2016. His wife, who inherited Contessa Entellina and chose the name, and their two children are living and are not named.

The 1851 cellars, the founding of 1983, the arrival on Pantelleria in 1989 and the Khamma winery opened to visitors in 2006 are the house's own pages; 1989 as Ben Ryé's first vintage and son of the wind are the house's sheets and several merchants (Terra Madre, The Wine Hub).
The queen of Naples is Maria Carolina in the house's telling; she is left unnamed for want of dates in two sources, and the story is hedged as the house's.

The making is the house's sheets, which vary by vintage: four to eight months in tank and ten to sixteen months in bottle, so the record gives the range; the dried grapes go into the must of a second, later picking by Terra Madre and the house's fresh must.

UNESCO's inscription of 2014 (9.COM, file 00720) is UNESCO's own page; its title calls the vine growing a traditional agricultural way of life in a word the house rules refuse, so the record says the island's way of growing its bush vines. The French address of the same page is cited, since the English one carries that word.
The library's style line calls the Pantelleria wines the serious end of the range and its wine record calls Ben Ryé the reference Passito di Pantelleria; neither ranking is repeated here.
Left out for want of a source: the names of the contrade the house farms on Pantelleria and the year of the Pantelleria DOC.

changed: story: "on the vineyards at Contessa Entellina that she had inherited from her father"; now "with the family's vineyards at Contessa Entellina, which she had taken in hand a few years before", as the house's roots page tells it (she took ownership and leadership of the family estate a few years earlier); no source read said she inherited it from her father.

story: "In 2006 it opened its Khamma winery on the island to visitors"; now "In 2008 it restored a walled Pantellerian garden at Khamma and gave it to FAI, the Italian national trust": no source read gave the opening of 2006, while the house's own page and FAI's page give the garden of 2008.

wine.making: "From the middle of August ... for three to four weeks" and "four to eight months in tank"; now "From August", the drying time cut, "stripped from their stalks by hand" added and "some months in tank": the house's sheets read give the first picking in the first half of August (2023) or from 17 August (2019), no sheet read gave three to four weeks, and the tank time runs four, five and seven months on the 2022, 2023 and 2016 sheets.
cards[0].back and questions[0].exp: "for three to four weeks" cut, for the same reason.

questions[1].exp: "from The Leopard, where Donnafugata, the woman in flight, recalls a queen's refuge"; now "from The Leopard, and the house ties its meaning, the woman in flight, to a fleeing queen", since the queen's refuge is the house's account of the name, not a scene of the novel.
open: The serving temperature follows the Codex's reference for sweet whites, 6 to 8 degrees; the house's own serving advice was not read.
Giacomo Rallo's dates rest on the house's own page (born in Marsala in 1937, died in 2016) and Decanter; his wife and children are living and stay unnamed.

records.place: Milo, on the eastern slope of Etna, Etna DOC, Sicily

wine.name: Etna Bianco Superiore Pietra Marina
wine.classification: Superiore: Etna Bianco from the commune of Milo alone, at least eighty per cent Carricante
wine.grapes: Carricante alone, where the Superiore rules ask for at least eighty per cent.
wine.sites: Old bush vines on small terraces walled with dry stone at Milo on Etna's eastern slope, in Contrada Rinazzo by the house's recent sheets, at about 800 metres, open to light, to the sea and to its winds.
wine.making: Picked by hand from the middle of October and pressed gently, the juice is fermented for about twelve days in temperature controlled stainless steel with a selected native yeast. The wine never sees oak: it rests two years and more on its fine lees in steel, stirred often, about thirty months by the recent sheets, then a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Lemon rind, green apple and white peach over chamomile, aniseed and the ash and wet stone of the volcano; lean and taut, with high, salty acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and citric for its first three to five years, it gains honey, beeswax and a smoky depth over a decade and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a white wine glass with room for its perfume.

label.means: Etna Bianco from the commune of Milo alone, with at least eighty per cent Carricante.
The volcano's denomination of 1968, the island's first DOC.
The house's name for its Carricante from Milo, first made with the 1990 vintage.

records.table: Benanti's Pietra Marina is Etna Bianco Superiore: Carricante from old terraced bush vines at Milo on the volcano's eastern face, kept for years on its lees in steel and never in oak. Lemon rind, ash and salty acidity: pour it cool, and give it years in bottle.
records.story: By the house's account a forebear made wine for his own pleasure at Viagrande, on the south eastern slope of Etna, at the end of the nineteenth century. In 1988 Giuseppe Benanti (1945 to 2023), born in Catania, founded a winery at Castiglione di Sicilia on the volcano's northern side, first called Tenuta di Castiglione. Few houses then bottled wine on Etna, whose DOC of 1968 had been the island's first, and the two harvests before 1990 went on trials of the mountain's grapes and slopes. The 1990 vintage gave the first wines to be bottled, among them Pietra Marina, Carricante from the terraces of Milo on the eastern face, the one commune whose white may be called Etna Bianco Superiore; it was shown at Vinitaly in 1993. In 1998, as the house tells it, the family added the old vineyards of Monte Serra at Viagrande, where its forebear had lived. In 2012 the founder handed the house to his twin sons, and he died in 2023. Pietra Marina is the white to open when a guest asks what Etna gives beyond its reds: Carricante from Milo, slow to open and long to live.

others.name: Rovittello
others.note: Etna Rosso of Nerello Mascalese from Castiglione di Sicilia on the northern slope, one of the house's first wines.

others.name: Serra della Contessa
others.note: Nerello Mascalese with Nerello Cappuccio from old vines at Monte Serra, on the south eastern slope.

traps: Etna Bianco Superiore may come only from the commune of Milo and needs at least eighty per cent Carricante; plain Etna Bianco needs sixty.
Many lists spell the wine Pietramarina; the house prints Pietra Marina, and it is not the house's Contrada Rinazzo, a separate Etna Bianco Superiore from the same contrada of Milo.
Benanti began in 1988 at Castiglione di Sicilia on the northern slope, not at Viagrande, where the family's forebear had made wine.

cards.front: Benanti's Pietra Marina: which grape, and from which commune?
cards.back: Carricante, from terraced bush vines at Milo on Etna's eastern slope.

cards.front: In what year, and on which side of Etna, was Benanti founded?
cards.back: In 1988, at Castiglione di Sicilia on the northern side, first as Tenuta di Castiglione.

questions.q: A guest asks why Benanti's Pietra Marina may call itself Etna Bianco Superiore. What do you tell them?
opts: It is Carricante grown in the commune of Milo
It spends at least two years in oak
It comes from vines above a thousand metres
It blends Carricante from every slope of Etna
questions.exp: The Superiore is kept for Etna Bianco from Milo with at least eighty per cent Carricante; height and oak are not the rule, and Pietra Marina sees steel alone.

questions.q: Benanti's first wines to be bottled, Pietra Marina among them, came from which vintage?
questions.exp: The first harvest was 1988 and the first bottled vintage 1990; 1968 is the year of the Etna DOC and 1998 the year the house added Monte Serra at Viagrande.

Benanti: Pietra Marina Etna Bianco Superiore technical sheet
AIS: Etna DOC production rules

report: Searches for this record: five of the group's 35 (two on the house's domain, three open); the house's profile sheets of 2020, 2023 and 2026 and its Pietra Marina sheet were read through search summaries.

Giuseppe Benanti's dates rest on the house's profile (born in Catania in July 1945, died at Viagrande in February 2023) and Wine Spectator (died 1 February 2023 aged 78). His twin sons, who took charge in 2012, are living and already in people.json; the oenologist he hired, also living, is not named.

The founding of 1988 at Castiglione di Sicilia as Tenuta di Castiglione rests on the house's profile and Wine Spectator. The library and plan call Benanti a Viagrande house of 1988, which holds for its later seat: the move to Viagrande and the Benanti name are dated 1998 by one account and the early 1990s by another, so the story gives 1998 only as the year the house added Monte Serra, by its own account.

The forebear at Viagrande is the founder's grandfather in the English sheets and his great grandfather in the Italian one, so he is a forebear; the branch's arrival from Bologna in 1734 is the house's claim alone and is left out.

Pietra Marina's sheet gives about 800 metres, the twelve day fermentation and about thirty months on the lees with a year in bottle; reviews of the 2011 and 2015 give 24 months, so the making says two years and more. Contrada Rinazzo rests on the house and Wilson Daniels; one merchant gave Contrada Caselle for the 2011, so the site is hedged as the recent sheets.
The library records the wine as Pietramarina; the house prints Pietra Marina, as the plan does, and the record follows the house.
Few houses bottling on Etna in 1988 rests on Wine Spectator (four wineries) and the library's revival line; the house's showing at Vinitaly in 1993 is its own profile.
The region record says Etna's DOCG was applied for in 2023 and still pending; nothing here depends on it.

changed: traps[1]: "Older lists spell the wine Pietramarina in one word; the house prints Pietra Marina, and it is the white, not one of the reds"; now "Many lists spell the wine Pietramarina; the house prints Pietra Marina, and it is not the house's Contrada Rinazzo, a separate Etna Bianco Superiore from the same contrada of Milo": Wine Spectator spelt it Pietramarina in 2023, so the spelling is not only an old one, and the house makes a separate Contrada Rinazzo Etna Bianco Superiore (its 2018 sheet), the nearer confusion now that the record names the contrada.
open: Old bush vines on terraces walled with dry stone rest on the author's reading of the house's sheet and Wilson Daniels; the refuter's searches gave the contrada, the 800 metres and the east facing slope but not the training.

The move of the house's seat to Viagrande and the change of name from Tenuta di Castiglione are dated about a decade after 1988 by Wine Spectator and 1998 by the house's timeline only for Monte Serra; the record dates only Monte Serra.

records.place: Contrada Samperi near Marsala, western Sicily

wine.name: Vecchio Samperi
wine.appellation: None: sold as wine outside the Marsala DOC
wine.grapes: Grillo alone, from the family's vineyards at Samperi.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards around the baglio in Contrada Samperi, about twelve kilometres from Marsala, on soils rich in limestone, with Grillo planted between 1970 and 1996.
wine.making: Grillo picked very ripe in the last week of September is pressed softly and fermented with wild yeasts in oak and chestnut barrels. The wine then joins a perpetuo begun at Samperi in 1978: the casks are never emptied, a little is drawn off each year and they are topped up with young wine. No spirit is added, and the blend averages fifteen years and more.
wine.glass: Walnut, toasted almond and dried apricot over bitter orange peel, iodine and sea salt; bone dry and warm, with a long, tangy finish that tastes of the casks.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, shaped already by its years in the perpetuo, and it keeps for many years in bottle.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold, as for a dry Oloroso; no need to decant; a small white wine glass.

label.means: Old Samperi: named for the contrada near Marsala where the family's baglio stands.
The house, named for its founder, who began the perpetuo at Samperi in 1978.

records.table: Marco De Bartoli's Vecchio Samperi is Grillo aged for years in a perpetuo of oak and chestnut casks at Samperi and never fortified, so it may not be called Marsala. Walnut, dried apricot and sea salt, bone dry: pour it cool as an aperitif or with aged cheese.
records.story: Marsala's trade with England began in 1773, and the wine shipped from the port was strengthened with spirit for the voyage. By most accounts the growers of the countryside had kept their own wine unfortified, drawing from casks they never emptied. At Samperi, the family's baglio about twelve kilometres from the town, where by the house's account vines and cellars go back over two centuries, Marco De Bartoli (1945 to 2011), a former racing driver, set out to make that older wine again. In 1978 he began a perpetuo of old Grillo, topping its casks each year with wine of very ripe grapes, and in 1980 he named its first bottling Vecchio Samperi. Since no spirit was added, the Marsala rules kept it from the name, and it was sold simply as wine. In 1984 he first bottled a passito on Pantelleria, at Bukkuram. In 1995 the Marsala prosecutors charged him with adulterating his wine; he was cleared five years later, the court finding that no offence had taken place. He died in 2011, and his children took the estate on. Vecchio Samperi is the bottle that tells a guest what Marsala was before the English: dry, oxidative and strong by nature alone.

others.name: Marsala Superiore Riserva
others.note: The house's fortified Marsala of Grillo, its case that the denomination can be serious.

others.name: Bukkuram
others.note: Passito di Pantelleria of sun dried Zibibbo, first bottled in 1984.

others.name: Vecchio Samperi Ventennale
others.note: A bottling of the same perpetuo with an average age of about twenty years.

traps: Vecchio Samperi is unfortified, so it cannot legally be called Marsala, whatever a list may print beside it.
Marsala tiers run Fine, Superiore, Superiore Riserva, Vergine and Vergine Stravecchio; Vecchio Samperi stands outside them all.
Bukkuram is De Bartoli's Passito di Pantelleria; do not confuse it with Donnafugata's Ben Ryé from the same island.

cards.front: Marco De Bartoli's Vecchio Samperi: why may it not be called Marsala?
cards.back: No spirit is added, and the Marsala rules ask for a fortified wine.

cards.front: What did the founder of Marco De Bartoli begin at Samperi in 1978?
cards.back: A perpetuo of old Grillo, its casks never emptied and topped up each year; its first bottling was named Vecchio Samperi in 1980.

questions.q: A guest sees Vecchio Samperi listed among the Marsalas. How do you explain where it belongs?
opts: An unfortified Grillo outside the Marsala DOC
A Marsala Vergine aged five years in wood
A Marsala Superiore sweetened with cooked must
A fortified Zibibbo from Pantelleria
questions.exp: Vecchio Samperi is Grillo aged in a perpetuo with no spirit added, so the Marsala rules exclude it; a Marsala Vergine, its nearest cousin, is a fortified wine.

questions.q: In 1995 the Marsala prosecutors brought a charge against Marco De Bartoli. How did it end?
opts: He was cleared five years later
He gave up the Samperi estate
He moved his cellar to Pantelleria
He agreed to fortify his wine
questions.exp: Charged with adulteration in 1995, he was cleared five years later, the court finding no offence; the family kept Samperi and its perpetuo.

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35 (three on the house's two domains, four open); the house's Vecchio Samperi, Quarantennale, Samperi, Bukkuram and founder pages were read through search summaries.

The founder's death on 18 March 2011 is the house's own page, which the region record agrees with; one Wine Spectator piece says 2010 and his birth is 1944 in some accounts and 1945 in others, so he is named, as the house is, with his death year only. His children are living and are not named.

The perpetuo begun in 1978 and the name Vecchio Samperi in 1980 are the house's pages, with Barberry and Primal Wine for the first release of 1980; the oak and chestnut casks the house's sheet and two merchants (Flatiron Wines, xtraWine); the average of about fifteen years is most merchants', with twenty in Primal Wine and an older xtraWine page, so the record says fifteen years and more.

The charge of adulteration in 1995 and the acquittal five years later rest on Balarm (no offence, il fatto non sussiste) and Barberry (the winery shut by the authorities from 1995 to 2000); the racing career on Barberry and Uncorked in Italy.
The trade of 1773 is the Codex's own (John Woodhouse); the unfortified perpetuo of the countryside before it rests on Flatiron Wines and the house's own account.

The label terms are kept to the wine's name and the house, since no source read settled what category the back label prints: the 2012 trip report on the house's site calls it a dry vino liquoroso, the Quarantennale sheet says fortified wine, and every other account says unfortified. The alcohol is 16.5 to 17.5 per cent by source and is left out.
The library's why calls Vecchio Samperi a great wine; that judgement is not repeated.

changed: story: "Marco De Bartoli, a former racing driver" with only his death year; now "Marco De Bartoli (1945 to 2011)", from the house's founder page (born in Marsala on 4 February 1945, died 2011), which WineNews and the Jancis Robinson obituary agree with (he died on 18 March 2011 aged 66).

story: "a baglio ... held by the family, as the house tells it, for over two centuries"; now "the family's baglio ... where by the house's account vines and cellars go back over two centuries", since the house's page says the vineyards and cellars have kept that memory for over two centuries, not that the family has held the baglio for that long.

questions[0].opts[1]: "A Marsala Vergine of the Soleras rank"; now "A Marsala Vergine aged five years in wood", since Soleras is another name for Vergine, not a rank of it (the Codex's Marsala records: Vergine, also labelled Soleras, at five years).
open: The average age of the perpetuo, fifteen years and more, rests on the author's merchants; the house's Italian sheet read here gives the vineyard's age, 20 to 42 years, not the blend's.
The racing career rests on the house's founder page, which lists car racing among the threads of his life, and the author's two merchants; no account read said what he raced.

records.place: Vittoria, in the province of Ragusa, Cerasuolo di Vittoria Classico DOCG, Sicily

wine.name: Cerasuolo di Vittoria Classico
wine.classification: Classico, the historic heart of Sicily's one DOCG, granted in 2005
wine.grapes: Nero d'Avola, about three fifths, with Frappato for the rest; the DOCG allows half to seven tenths Nero d'Avola.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards around its cellar outside Vittoria, about 230 metres up, on red sand and clay over limestone that lies thirty to sixty centimetres below the surface.
wine.making: The grapes are fermented on their skins with native yeasts, in concrete tanks by most merchants' sheets, and the house makes it without chemical additions. The wine then ages in large casks of Slavonian oak, a year to eighteen months by most sheets, some vintages with a further spell in concrete; the DOCG holds a Classico back until 31 March of the second year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, red plum and pomegranate over rose petal, white pepper and dried orange peel; medium bodied, with fine, light tannin, fresh acidity and a savoury, dusty finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fragrant within three or four years of the harvest, it gains dried cherry and leather over a decade in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with air; a Burgundy bowl.

label.means: Nero d'Avola with Frappato from around Vittoria: a DOC from 1973 and Sicily's one DOCG from 2005.
The historic inner zone, held back until 31 March of the second year after the harvest.
Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, the rank above DOC in Italian wine law.

records.table: COS's Cerasuolo di Vittoria Classico is Nero d'Avola with Frappato from red sand over limestone outside Vittoria, fermented with native yeasts and aged in large oak casks. Sour cherry, pomegranate and white pepper on light tannin: pour it a little cool, even with tuna.
records.story: In 1980 three young friends of Vittoria made wine together for the first time, in the old cellar of one of their families and from vines his father gave them. The house's name joins the initials of their three surnames. Their first vintage, picked on 5 October 1980, filled fewer than fifteen hundred bottles. In 1985 one of the three left for medicine and his sister took his share. Cerasuolo di Vittoria, the red of Nero d'Avola and Frappato from the red sands of the south east, had been a DOC since 1973, and the friends set out to make it as cleanly as they could, with native yeasts and no chemical additions. In September 2000 their first clay amphorae arrived from Spain, and Pithos, a wine fermented and aged in jars set into the ground, was born. In 2005 Cerasuolo di Vittoria became Sicily's first DOCG, and the house says its wine was the first to carry the new name. COS's Classico is the bottle to pour when a guest asks for Sicily's one DOCG: paler and more perfumed than the island's reputation, and made with a light hand.

others.name: Pithos Rosso
others.note: Nero d'Avola with Frappato fermented and aged in clay amphorae set into the ground, first made in 2000.

traps: Cerasuolo di Vittoria is a red DOCG of Sicily; Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a rosato of Montepulciano.
COS is the initials of its three founders, not a place, and has nothing to do with Château Cos d'Estournel of Saint-Estèphe.
Classico is the historic inner zone of the DOCG and waits longer before release than plain Cerasuolo di Vittoria, which may leave on 1 June of the year after the harvest.

cards.front: COS: where does the name of the house come from?
cards.back: The initials of the surnames of the three friends who founded it in 1980.

cards.front: Cerasuolo di Vittoria: what share of Nero d'Avola do the DOCG rules allow, and what is the rest?
cards.back: Half to seven tenths Nero d'Avola, the rest Frappato; COS's Classico runs about three fifths Nero d'Avola.

questions.q: A guest asks what makes COS's Cerasuolo di Vittoria Classico lighter than most Sicilian reds. Which answer fits?
opts: Frappato blended with Nero d'Avola
Nerello Mascalese from high on Etna
A long rest under flor yeast
Grapes dried in the sun before pressing
questions.exp: The DOCG blends Nero d'Avola with thirty to fifty per cent Frappato, a pale, perfumed grape; Nerello Mascalese is Etna's grape and has no place in Cerasuolo.

questions.q: In what year did Cerasuolo di Vittoria, the wine COS's founders set out to make cleanly in 1980, become a DOCG?
questions.exp: It was a DOC from 1973 and became a DOCG by decree in 2005; 2000 is the year the house's first amphorae arrived from Spain.

report: Searches for this record: five of the group's 35 (two on the house's domain, three open); the house's company page, its Cerasuolo and Pithos page and its press archive were read through search summaries.

The three founders (Giambattista Cilia, Giusto Occhipinti, both in people.json, and Cirino Strano), the sister who took Strano's share in 1985 and the founder's father who gave the cellar and vines are living or undated and are not named; one house page gives the third founder's name differently.

The first harvest of 5 October 1980 and its 1,470 bottles, the amphorae from Spain in September 2000 and the DOCG wine of 2005 are the house's pages, with Primal Wine and Coppiera beside them; the first wine to carry the DOCG is the house's claim and is told as such.

The DOC of 29 May 1973 and the DOCG of 13 September 2005 rest on Wikipedia and Wein.plus beside the Codex; the shares, the release dates (31 March of the second year for Classico, 1 June of the next year otherwise) and the Classico zone rest on the AIS copy of the disciplinare.

The making is uncertain: most merchants (Flatiron Wines, Astor Wines, Beaune Imports) give fermentation in concrete with native yeasts and ageing in large old oak casks for 18 months in one account, 24 in another and a year in wood and a year in concrete in a third, while one importer gives co-fermentation in amphora for the 2022 and one profile says the cellar used only amphorae from the 2007 harvest. The record says concrete by most sheets and large casks for a year to two; the integrator may wish to settle it.

The 230 metres and the red sand and clay over limestone rest on the house's pages (limestone thirty to sixty centimetres down) and Beaune Imports; the library's biodynamic farming is not repeated, since the house's pages read here say organic.
Left out: the founders' ages and studies in 1980, which the sources give differently, and the Classico delle Fontane, on one merchant alone.

changed: story: "from bush vines his father gave them"; now "from vines his father gave them", since the house's company page says the family cellar and vineyard were passed to them by one founder's father and gives no training.

wine.making: "ages in large old oak casks for a year to two"; now "ages in large casks of Slavonian oak, a year to eighteen months by most sheets, some vintages with a further spell in concrete", since the merchants read give eighteen months in Slavonian botti or a year in botti and a year in concrete, the two years in wood belong to the separate Bastonaca bottling, and no sheet read said the casks were old; "in concrete" is now "in concrete tanks".
table: "aged in large old casks"; now "aged in large oak casks", for the same reason.
open: The house's own page dates the DOC to 1974; the decree is of 29 May 1973, published on 28 August 1973 (AIS copy of the rules, Wikipedia), and the record keeps 1973.
One importer gives fermentation in amphora for the 2022 vintage; the record keeps concrete tanks by most sheets, and the integrator may wish to settle it from the house's sheet.
